paras: The threatened lynching of Sam Long refers to a September 1888 report that Long, a Black man from Georgia held by officers at Eufaula, Alabama, would likely be lynched if returned to Miller County, Georgia, where he was wanted on a charge of assaulting a white woman. The only report found, a brief in the Savannah Morning News, said his chances for a trial were "thought to be slim"; no account of his fate appears in the coverage.

According to the report, Long had worked for more than a year for the husband of the woman he was accused of assaulting. He was charged with luring her out, while her husband was away, to see a horse he said was sick, assaulting her, and then trying to force her to take poison. The alleged assault took place "last October," and the husband offered a reward of $100.

Long had eluded officials for months until his whereabouts were discovered "a few days" before the September 5, 1888, report. Officers Rhody and Brown arrested him at Eufaula and held him until an order could be obtained from the governor to turn him over to the Miller County authorities. Long denied the charge and said his name was Josh, not Sam, though the paper said he "answers to the description fully."
The reward was to go to the two arresting officers. No report of his delivery to Georgia, a trial, or a lynching was found in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News carried the story on page 6 among short items of Georgia news, between a fish story and a church anecdote. The paragraph called Long "a Georgia negro" and the woman "a white lady," and it narrated the alleged crime as fact while also noting his denial. It closed by treating the prospect of a lynching as routine: "it is intimated that he will be lynched on sight in Miller county," without saying who had made the intimation. No other paper's account was found.

accounts.label: Georgia news brief
accounts.gist: Long was held at Eufaula for return to Miller county on a charge of assaulting his employer's wife and trying to poison her; he denied it, and it was 'intimated' he would be lynched on sight in Miller county.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran it among state briefs, narrating the alleged crime as fact while noting his denial, and treated the prospect of lynching matter-of-factly ('His chances for a trial are thought to be slim').
